title: Three Tips for Building Trust and Preventing Zombie Burnout
author: Regenerative Schools
summary: A new principal recounts committing to 57 individual one-on-one meetings with staff during a transition plan, driven by the conviction that 'being listened to is so close to being loved that for the average person, they are almost indistinguishable.' The piece frames genuine listening as a skill the author still struggles with, and argues that deliberately designing one's technology environment — not willpower alone — is what actually makes deep listening possible. The three concrete tactics are: turning off nearly all phone notifications so a supervisor isn't visibly distracted mid-meeting; limiting email checks to two or three times a day, including keeping the laptop closed during one-on-ones; and, seemingly in tension with the first two, using gentle phone alarms five minutes before each meeting so punctuality worries don't compete for attention during the conversation itself. The author connects this practice directly to burnout research by Christina Maslach and Michael Leiter, which identifies lack of voice or autonomy as a key driver of teacher burnout, arguing that deep listening sessions build the trust and sense of being heard that counteracts it. The piece closes by naming the cost of the alternative — Brad Stulberg's 'zombie burnout,' the restless, unfulfilled exhaustion of a day spent reacting to notifications — and frames intentional tech design as necessary for both staff and the leader's own flourishing.

quotes: Being listened to is so close to being loved that for the average person, they are almost indistinguishable.” —David Ausburger
For me, listening is harder than talking. Slowing down is harder than speeding up. And being present is harder than being distracted.
If I’m going to ask someone that I supervise to schedule a one-on-one meeting with me, but then I am distracted and checking my phone, we might as well not have met at all.
Christina Maslach and Michael Leiter, burnout researchers, found that lack of autonomy, or a sense that you don’t have a voice in your workplace, is one key driver of burnout.
When I spend too many hours on email or being interrupted with notifications, I end the day feeling what Brad Stulberg calls “zombie burnout.

Answering email and responding to notifications might give me a quick hit of dopamine in the moment. But in the long term, constant interruptions make me feel restless and exhausted, distracted and unfulfilled.
When you design your tech environment intentionally, you make space for both your staff and yourself to flourish. Regenerative schools require nothing less.
